name: Pyramid
function: Ventral surface bundle of the medulla formed by corticospinal fibers descending from the basis pontis, flanking the anterior median fissure; at the cervicomedullary junction roughly 85-90 percent of its axons cross in the pyramidal decussation to become the lateral corticospinal tract, the remainder continuing as the anterior corticospinal tract.

afferent: Corticospinal fibers descending through the basis pontis (before the pyramidal decussation)
efferent: Crossed fibers through the pyramidal decussation (tract-pyramidal-decussation) to the lateral corticospinal tract; an uncrossed minority continues in the anterior corticospinal pathway

bloodSupply: Paramedian vertebral branches, especially rostrally, and anterior spinal artery branches, especially caudally; territories overlap.

clinical.findings: A unilateral lesion of the pyramid above the motor decussation can cause contralateral arm and leg weakness, usually sparing the face. Associated ipsilateral tongue weakness suggests extension to hypoglossal fascicles in medial medullary syndrome.

Corticospinal weakness contralateral to a brainstem lesion can accompany an ipsilateral cranial nerve deficit when both pathways are involved. The pattern depends on lesion extent and is not required in every brainstem lesion.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 6, corticospinal pathways, printed pp. 230-233 (PDF pp. 256-259).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), motor and sensory decussation sections, printed pp. 108-110 (PDF pp. 122-124).
Lemon and Morecraft, The evidence against somatotopic organization of function in the primate corticospinal tract, Brain 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36575147/.

name: Pyramidal decussation
function: The great motor crossover at the cervicomedullary junction: the majority of corticospinal axons sweep posteromedially across the midline, interrupting the anterior median fissure, so that each cerebral hemisphere commands the opposite half of the body. The crossing fibers remodel the internal architecture of the closed medulla, displacing the gray matter laterally.

afferent: Pyramids (tract-pyramid)
efferent: Contralateral lateral corticospinal tract of the spinal cord (tract-corticospinal-lateral)

bloodSupply: Anterior spinal artery and vertebral branches

clinical.findings: Injury at the pyramidal decussation can cause complex unilateral or bilateral weakness. Arm-predominant cruciate paralysis has been described after cervicomedullary injury, but a fixed arm-versus-leg crossing order should not be presented as established.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 6, corticospinal pathways, printed pp. 230-233 (PDF pp. 256-259).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), motor and sensory decussation sections, printed pp. 108-110 (PDF pp. 122-124).
Lemon and Morecraft, The evidence against somatotopic organization of function in the primate corticospinal tract, Brain 2023, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36575147/.

name: Internal arcuate fibers
function: The sensory decussation: second-order axons of the gracile and cuneate nuclei sweep ventromedially around the central gray, cross the midline as a broad sheet ventral to the central canal, and pivot rostrally to form the contralateral medial lemniscus — the handoff at which each medial lemniscus comes to represent the opposite half of the body.

afferent: Nucleus gracilis (nuc-nucleus-gracilis)
Nucleus cuneatus (nuc-nucleus-cuneatus)
efferent: Contralateral medial lemniscus (tract-medial-lemniscus) ascending to VPL

bloodSupply: Anterior spinal artery and vertebral perforators

clinical.findings: Dorsal-column or gracile/cuneate nuclear injury before the crossing causes ipsilateral loss of vibration and position sense; medial lemniscal injury after the crossing causes contralateral loss. Lesions involving the crossing fibers may affect both sides.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, posterior column-medial lemniscal pathway, printed pp. 276-280 (PDF pp. 302-306).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), closed medulla and sensory decussation, printed pp. 108-112 (PDF pp. 122-126).

name: Fasciculus gracilis
function: Medial dorsal-column bundle conveying, uncrossed and somatotopically ordered, large-fiber touch, vibration, two-point discrimination and conscious proprioception from the lower limb and lower trunk (below about T6) up to the nucleus gracilis; medial in the dorsal funiculus at every cord and lower-medullary level.

afferent: Dorsal root (large-fiber) afferents of the lower trunk and lower limb ascending ipsilaterally
efferent: Nucleus gracilis (nuc-nucleus-gracilis)

bloodSupply: Posterior spinal artery (dorsal medullary branches)

clinical.findings: Injury to this pre-crossing dorsal-column pathway can impair ipsilateral lower-body vibration, joint position and discriminative touch. Sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg sign may occur; the extent depends on lesion size and other sensory pathways.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, posterior column-medial lemniscal pathway, printed pp. 276-280 (PDF pp. 302-306).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), closed medulla and sensory decussation, printed pp. 108-112 (PDF pp. 122-126).

name: Nucleus gracilis
function: First synapse of the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway for the lower body: primary afferents of the fasciculus gracilis terminate in somatotopically organised (leg-arranged) columns, and the second-order neurons emit the internal arcuate fibers that decussate to form the contralateral medial lemniscus. Its dorsal bulge is the gracile tubercle of the closed medulla.

afferent: Fasciculus gracilis (tract-fasciculus-gracilis)
efferent: Internal arcuate fibers (tract-internal-arcuate) to the contralateral medial lemniscus

bloodSupply: Posterior spinal artery; PICA medial branches

clinical.findings: Injury to the gracile nucleus affects lower-limb/lower-trunk vibration, position sense and discriminative touch on the ipsilateral side because its second-order axons have not yet crossed. Contralateral deficits localize downstream to the medial lemniscus.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, posterior column-medial lemniscal pathway, printed pp. 276-280 (PDF pp. 302-306).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), closed medulla and sensory decussation, printed pp. 108-112 (PDF pp. 122-126).

name: Fasciculus cuneatus
function: Lateral dorsal-column bundle conveying uncrossed large-fiber touch, vibration and proprioception from the upper trunk, upper limb and neck (above about T6) to the nucleus cuneatus; present only above midthoracic levels, lying lateral to the fasciculus gracilis throughout the upper cord and closed medulla.

afferent: Upper trunk, upper limb and neck dorsal-root large-fiber afferents
efferent: Nucleus cuneatus (nuc-nucleus-cuneatus)

bloodSupply: Posterior spinal artery (dorsal medullary branches)

clinical.findings: Pre-crossing pathway injury can impair ipsilateral upper-limb/upper-trunk vibration, position and discriminative touch. A restricted lesion may spare lower-body pathways; pseudoathetosis and a positive Romberg sign are possible rather than required.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, posterior column-medial lemniscal pathway, printed pp. 276-280 (PDF pp. 302-306).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), closed medulla and sensory decussation, printed pp. 108-112 (PDF pp. 122-126).

name: Nucleus cuneatus
function: Principal dorsal-column relay for vibration, conscious proprioception and discriminative touch from the upper body. It lies lateral to the gracile nucleus in the dorsal caudal medulla, and its axons cross as internal arcuate fibers to form the contralateral medial lemniscus. The adjacent accessory (external) cuneate nucleus is a distinct nucleus that supplies the cuneocerebellar pathway.

afferent: Fasciculus cuneatus (tract-fasciculus-cuneatus) from ipsilateral upper trunk and upper limb
efferent: Internal arcuate fibers (tract-internal-arcuate) to the contralateral medial lemniscus

bloodSupply: Posterior spinal artery; PICA medial branches

clinical.findings: Principal cuneate nuclear lesions can impair ipsilateral upper-limb vibration, position sense and discriminative touch before the sensory decussation. Accessory cuneate injury can instead affect unconscious proprioceptive input to the cerebellum.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, posterior column-medial lemniscal pathway, printed pp. 276-280 (PDF pp. 302-306).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), closed medulla and sensory decussation, printed pp. 108-112 (PDF pp. 122-126).

name: Principal inferior olivary nucleus
function: Folded gray lamella of the inferior olivary complex forming the ventrolateral medullary olive. Along with the accessory olivary nuclei, it provides crossed olivocerebellar climbing fibers through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to Purkinje cells and participates in timing and motor learning. The principal olive receives rubro-olivary input through the central tegmental tract.

afferent: Red nucleus via the central tegmental tract (tract-central-tegmental, rubro-olivary fibers)
Nucleo-olivary fibers from the dentate and interposed nuclei
Spino-olivary and trigeminal afferents
efferent: Olivocerebellar climbing fibers crossing through the inferior cerebellar peduncle (tract-icp) to the contralateral cerebellar cortex

bloodSupply: Direct branches of the vertebral artery; ASA and PICA borderzone

clinical.findings: Transsynaptic degeneration of the olive after a lesion of the Guillain-Mollaret triangle (dentate nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle, or central tegmental tract), producing palatal (palatopharyngeal) myoclonus/tremor months after the index lesion.
clinical.note: MRI shows T2 hyperintensity with enlargement of the olive (hypertrophic degeneration, not atrophy).

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar nuclei and connections, printed pp. 698-710 (PDF pp. 724-736).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medulla and inferior olive, printed pp. 112-121 (PDF pp. 126-135).

name: Medial accessory olivary nucleus
function: Medial accessory subdivision of the inferior olivary complex, medial to the principal olive. It contributes climbing fibers to contralateral cerebellar cortical zones through the inferior cerebellar peduncle, participating with other olivary subdivisions in cerebellar sensorimotor learning.

afferent: Spinal, brainstem and cerebellar nucleo-olivary inputs; detailed subnuclear projection patterns are not represented in this schematic
efferent: Crossed olivocerebellar climbing fibers through the inferior cerebellar peduncle (tract-icp) to contralateral cerebellar cortex

bloodSupply: Vertebral artery branches; ASA borderzone

clinical.findings: Inferior olivary lesions or deafferentation can disrupt cerebellar function. Hypertrophic olivary degeneration and symptomatic palatal tremor are associated with disruption of dentato-rubro-olivary circuitry; those findings should not be localized specifically to this accessory subdivision from this atlas.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar nuclei and connections, printed pp. 698-710 (PDF pp. 724-736).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medulla and inferior olive, printed pp. 112-121 (PDF pp. 126-135).

name: Medial lemniscus
function: Ascending second-order dorsal-column pathway formed by crossed internal arcuate fibers, carrying vibration, proprioception and discriminative touch from the contralateral body to VPL. In the medulla the upright ribbon has lower-body fibers ventrally and upper-body fibers dorsally; with ascent into the pons it rotates so that lower-body fibers lie more laterally. Its position changes across brainstem levels.

afferent: Internal arcuate fibers (tract-internal-arcuate) from the gracile and cuneate nuclei
efferent: Ventral posterolateral nucleus (nuc-vpl), thence S1 (tract-dcml composite pathway)

bloodSupply: Paramedian vertebral/anterior spinal branches in the medulla, basilar perforators in the pons, and proximal PCA/basilar-apex branches in the midbrain.

clinical.findings: Damage after the sensory decussation can reduce contralateral vibration, joint-position sense and discriminative touch; sensory ataxia may occur. Brainstem level is determined by associated cranial nerve and long-tract findings, not this deficit alone.

A lesion affecting both the medial lemniscus and neighboring descending motor or cerebellar pathways may combine contralateral sensory loss, weakness and ataxia. Ataxic hemiparesis has several possible anatomical substrates.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 7, posterior column-medial lemniscal pathway, printed pp. 276-280 (PDF pp. 302-306).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), closed medulla and sensory decussation, printed pp. 108-112 (PDF pp. 122-126).

name: Spinal trigeminal tract
function: Descending primary sensory fibers entering with CN V at the lateral pons and traveling beside the spinal trigeminal nucleus into the medulla and upper cervical cord. They carry facial pain, temperature and some crude touch, with small general sensory contributions from CN VII, IX and X. V1, V2 and V3 have ventral-to-dorsal organization, distinct from the rostral-to-caudal concentric facial representation.

afferent: Primary sensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglion, with general sensory contributions from peripheral ganglia of CN VII, IX and X
efferent: Spinal trigeminal nucleus (nuc-spinal-trigeminal)

bloodSupply: PICA and vertebral lateral medullary branches

clinical.findings: Lateral medullary or pontine lesions can cause ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss, sometimes with relative preservation of discriminative touch. The distribution depends on which fibers and nuclear subdivisions are affected; an onion-skin pattern is possible but not obligatory.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, trigeminal sensory system, printed pp. 508-512 (PDF pp. 534-538).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medullary sections, printed pp. 108-118 (PDF pp. 122-132).

name: Spinal trigeminal nucleus
function: Long column of second-order facial pain-temperature neurons (subnuclei oralis, interpolaris and caudalis) extending from the caudal pons through the medulla into the upper cervical cord; subnucleus caudalis is the lamina-like pain relay (comparable to the spinal dorsal horn), while rostral parts gate corneal-blink and other trigeminal reflex arcs. Output rises through the ventral trigeminothalamic tract to contralateral VPM.

afferent: Spinal trigeminal tract (tract-spinal-trigeminal) afferents of CN V, VII, IX, X
efferent: Ventral trigeminothalamic tract (tract-trigeminothalamic-ventral)
Reflex interneurons to the facial motor nucleus (blink) and ambiguus (gag)

bloodSupply: PICA / vertebral lateral branches; AICA rostrally

clinical.syndrome: Ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss and impaired corneal reflex
clinical.findings: Damage can reduce ipsilateral facial nociception and the afferent component of the corneal blink reflex. Concentric facial sensory loss may occur because perioral regions are represented more rostrally and peripheral facial regions more caudally. The gag reflex is primarily a CN IX-X circuit and is not a specific test of this nucleus.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, trigeminal sensory system, printed pp. 508-512 (PDF pp. 534-538).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medullary sections, printed pp. 108-118 (PDF pp. 122-132).

name: Nucleus solitarius (cardiorespiratory part)
function: The visceral afferent hub of the dorsomedial medulla: first synapse for CN IX and CN X general visceral afferents — carotid-body chemoreceptors and carotid-sinus baroreceptors, aortic arch receptors, pulmonary stretch fibers, laryngeal-pharyngeal sensation and gastrointestinal afferents. Its neurons compute the reflexes controlling blood pressure, respiration, swallowing and GI motility, and project to the dorsal motor vagal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus and the ventrolateral medullary vasomotor/respiratory columns.

afferent: CN IX carotid body/sinus and pharyngeal afferents
CN X aortic, pulmonary, laryngeal and gastrointestinal afferents
efferent: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (nuc-dmv)
Nucleus ambiguus (nuc-ambiguus) for swallow/gag motor arc
Ventrolateral medulla (respiratory and vasomotor columns)
Hypothalamus and parabrachial nuclei (visceral-limbic relay)

bloodSupply: PICA (dorsolateral medullary branches); vertebral artery

clinical.findings: NTS-region injury can impair visceral afferent processing, baroreflex control and swallowing/airway protection. Medullary strokes may produce blood-pressure or respiratory instability, especially with neighboring autonomic circuitry involved; the direction and severity are not fixed by an isolated nucleus label.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), open medulla and cranial nerve nuclei, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).

name: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (CN X)
function: Preganglionic parasympathetic nucleus beneath the vagal trigone in the dorsomedial medulla. Its axons travel in CN X to ganglia near thoracic and abdominal viscera, particularly controlling gastrointestinal motility and secretion. Cardiac vagal control also has an important source in the nucleus ambiguus and should not be assigned solely to the DMV.

afferent: Nucleus solitarius (nuc-solitarius-caudal) baroreceptor-visceral input
Hypothalamic autonomic descending fibers
efferent: Vagal preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to cardiac, pulmonary and enteric ganglia

bloodSupply: PICA and ASA-vertebral branches (dorsomedial medulla)

clinical.findings: Dorsal vagal complex injury can disturb gastrointestinal motility and visceral reflexes. Swallowing and vocal-fold weakness in medullary syndromes primarily reflect ambiguus branchiomotor involvement; bradycardia or asystole is not the predictable result of simply losing DMV parasympathetic neurons.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), open medulla and cranial nerve nuclei, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).

name: Nucleus ambiguus
function: Medullary branchiomotor neurons supplying stylopharyngeus through CN IX and palatal, pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles through CN X. Fibers historically called the cranial root of CN XI are functionally part of vagal outflow. The ambiguus region also contains cardiac parasympathetic neurons; its branchiomotor connections support swallowing, phonation and airway protection.

afferent: Solitary and reticular networks involved in swallowing and gag reflexes
Predominantly bilateral corticobulbar input
Respiratory pattern-generator inputs
efferent: CN IX to stylopharyngeus
CN X to palate, pharynx and larynx
Cardiac preganglionic vagal fibers

bloodSupply: PICA (lateral medullary branches)

clinical.findings: Unilateral nucleus/fascicle injury can produce ipsilateral palatal and vocal-fold weakness, hoarseness and dysphagia, with aspiration risk. Severity varies with lesion extent and compensating pathways.

Degeneration of ambiguus, hypoglossal and other bulbar motor neurons can cause progressive dysarthria and dysphagia. Bilateral corticobulbar disease causes a different, supranuclear pattern, often with spastic speech and emotional lability.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), open medulla and cranial nerve nuclei, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).

name: Hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII)
function: Paramedian column of LMNs under the hypoglossal trigone of the ventricular floor innervating all intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles except the palatoglossus; its bulge helps shape the floor of the fourth ventricle. Corticobulbar input to hypoglossal motoneurons (notably genioglossus) is predominantly contralateral.

afferent: Corticobulbar fibers (contralateral-dominant, genioglossus)
Solitary and reticular viscerosensory inputs (taste-driven feeding reflexes)
efferent: CN XII rootlets through the preolivary sulcus (surf-cn12-exit) to tongue musculature

bloodSupply: Paramedian vertebral and anterior spinal artery branches, with regional overlap.

clinical.findings: Nuclear/fascicular injury can cause ipsilateral tongue weakness and deviation toward the weak side on protrusion. Atrophy/fasciculations depend on denervation and time. Bilateral injury may severely impair speech and oral bolus movement; complete immobility is not obligatory.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), open medulla and cranial nerve nuclei, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).

name: Area postrema
function: Paired circumventricular organ flanking the obex at the caudal floor of the fourth ventricle; because it lacks a blood-brain barrier, it samples blood-borne toxins, drugs and circulating cytokines and triggers the vomiting reflex through the adjacent solitary nucleus and medullary reticular-vagal emetic circuitry — the neural chemoreceptor trigger zone.

afferent: Blood-borne and CSF-borne chemical signals (no blood-brain barrier)
Vagal afferents via the solitary nucleus
efferent: Nucleus solitarius (nuc-solitarius-caudal)
Medullary reticular emetic pattern generators and dorsal vagal complex

bloodSupply: PICA inferior medial branches (permeable capillaries)

clinical.findings: Lesions in the area-postrema region can cause otherwise unexplained persistent nausea, vomiting or hiccups. Vertigo is not intrinsic to the area postrema and suggests additional vestibular involvement. The region is also a recognized site of inflammatory injury, including neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, motor/autonomic reticular systems, printed pp. 646-648 (PDF pp. 672-674).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medullary nuclei, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).
Wingerchuk et al., International consensus diagnostic criteria for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders, Neurology 2015, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26092914/.

name: Inferior cerebellar peduncle
function: The dominant afferent gateway of the cerebellum: the dorsolateral column formed in the upper medulla by olivocerebellar climbing fibers, cuneocerebellar and posterior spinocerebellar fibers, vestibulocerebellar fibers and reticulocerebellar fibers, all entering the vermis and hemispheres; the juxtarestiform body carries the vestibular portion.

afferent: Crossed climbing fibers from the inferior olivary complex
Cuneocerebellar fibers from the accessory (external) cuneate nucleus, distinct from the principal cuneate nucleus
Posterior spinocerebellar tract (tract-posterior-spinocerebellar)
Vestibular and reticular afferents
efferent: Afferent fibers terminate in cerebellar cortex and deep nuclei
Juxtarestiform body also carries cerebellar efferents to vestibular and reticular nuclei

bloodSupply: PICA and vertebral circumferential branches

clinical.findings: Restiform-body injury can cause ipsilateral limb dysmetria and gait ataxia. Adjacent vestibular involvement adds vertigo and nystagmus; a small lateral medullary stroke may initially resemble a peripheral vestibular disorder. Clinical findings alone in this schematic do not exclude stroke.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar nuclei and connections, printed pp. 698-710 (PDF pp. 724-736).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medulla and inferior olive, printed pp. 112-121 (PDF pp. 126-135).

name: Arcuate nucleus (medulla)
function: Small cell groups on the ventral medullary surface near the pyramids. They are associated with external arcuate projections toward the cerebellum; proposed respiratory chemosensory roles are not established sufficiently to infer a specific human lesion syndrome from this nucleus alone.

afferent: Corticofugal descending fibers
Medullary surface chemoreceptive afferents
efferent: Ventral external arcuate fibers to the contralateral cerebellum via tract-icp

bloodSupply: Anterior spinal artery / vertebral branches

clinical.findings: Ventral medullary injury may affect multiple motor and respiratory pathways. An isolated arcuate-nucleus lesion is not an established explanation for congenital central hypoventilation syndrome, which is associated with pathogenic PHOX2B variants and impaired autonomic development.

refs: Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), arcuate nucleus on the ventral medullary surface, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).
GeneReviews, Congenital Central Hypoventilation Syndrome, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1427/ (PHOX2B-associated disorder).

name: Medullary reticular formation
synonyms: medullary reticular nuclei (gigantocellular, central, ventral and dorsal) — this record covers the formation as a whole
function: Gigantocellular and central-medial reticular nuclei filling the intermediate tegmentum: source of the medullary (lateral) reticulospinal tract that inhibits antigravity tone and refines posture, site of ventrolateral respiratory column and vasomotor (pressure) integration with the solitary nucleus, and upward continuation of the reticular activating system; premotor autonomic fibers descend to the spinal intermediolateral column.

afferent: Spinoreticular tract (tract-spinoreticular)
Nucleus solitarius (nuc-solitarius-caudal)
Fastigial nucleus (nuc-fastigial)
Hypothalamic and periaqueductal descending fibers
efferent: Medullary reticulospinal tract (tract-reticulospinal)
Ascending arousal projections to the intralaminar thalamic nuclei
Premotor autonomic fibers to spinal sympathetic neurons

bloodSupply: Vertebral and PICA branches; ASA paramedian branches

clinical.findings: Medullary reticular/ventrolateral respiratory and vasomotor network injury can disturb automatic breathing and cardiovascular regulation. The manifestations depend on which neuronal groups and descending pathways are affected.
Injury to descending sympathetic fibers in the lateral medullary tegmentum can produce ipsilateral mild ptosis, miosis and variable anhidrosis.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 14, motor/autonomic reticular systems, printed pp. 646-648 (PDF pp. 672-674).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medullary nuclei, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).
Wingerchuk et al., International consensus diagnostic criteria for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders, Neurology 2015, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26092914/.

name: Fourth ventricle
function: CSF cavity between dorsal pons/open medulla and cerebellum, with its floor in the rhomboid fossa. CSF enters from the cerebral aqueduct and exits through the median aperture (Magendie) and paired lateral apertures (Luschka) into the subarachnoid space; the central canal continues caudally.

clinical.findings: Tumors of the floor or roof (ependymoma, medulloblastoma) or outflow blockage of Luschka/Magendie trap CSF and raise intracranial pressure with headache, vomiting and papilledema.
clinical.note: The choroid plexus of the roof (tela choroidea) is a principal CSF production site of the posterior fossa.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 5, ventricles and CSF, printed pp. 132-137 (PDF pp. 158-163).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 5, hydrocephalus, printed pp. 155-156 (PDF pp. 181-182).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), ventricular system, printed pp. 66-69 (PDF pp. 80-83).
bloodSupply: The ventricular lumen is not perfused tissue. Surrounding brainstem/cerebellar tissue and fourth-ventricular choroid plexus have separate variable vertebrobasilar/PICA/AICA/SCA supplies.

name: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) exit
function: Rootlets of CN IX emerging from the postolivary sulcus just rostral to the vagal rows: motor fibers to stylopharyngeus (from the nucleus ambiguus), parasympathetic fibers to the parotid (inferior salivatory) and afferents for oropharyngeal sensation, tonsil-posterior tongue taste and carotid sinus-body baroreceptor-chemoreceptor information — the afferent limb of the gag reflex.

clinical.findings: Root injury can impair pharyngeal/posterior tongue sensation or taste and IX gag-reflex afference. Normal gag responses vary; obligatory carotid reflex failure and fixed blood-pressure changes cannot be inferred.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), open medulla and cranial nerve nuclei, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).

name: Vagus nerve (CN X) exit
function: Rows of vagal rootlets leaving the postolivary sulcus below CN IX, carrying fibers from the dorsal motor nucleus (parasympathetic viscera), nucleus ambiguus (palate-pharynx-larynx striated muscle) and returning visceral afferents from thoracic and abdominal viscera through the solitary complex.

clinical.findings: Vagal motor root involvement can cause palatal/vocal-fold weakness, dysphagia and hoarseness. Sensory or autonomic features depend on affected fibers and lesion extent.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), open medulla and cranial nerve nuclei, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).

name: Accessory nerve (CN XI) exit
synonyms: cranial and spinal roots of CN XI
function: Spinal accessory rootlets arise from the upper cervical cord and ascend through the foramen magnum before leaving through the jugular foramen to supply sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Nearby caudal medullary rootlets historically termed the cranial root of XI travel with the vagus and are best understood functionally as CN X, rather than the source of shoulder motor fibers.

clinical.findings: Unilateral CN XI damage wastes ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid (weak contralateral head rotation) and trapezius (shoulder droop, scapular winging); foramen magnum and jugular foramen lesions are the classic localizers.
clinical.note: The spinal rootlets climbing the lateral medulla are tagged on the closed-medulla plates.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), open medulla and cranial nerve nuclei, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).

name: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) exit
function: Rootlets of CN XII emerging between pyramid and olive at the preolivary sulcus and collecting into the hypoglossal nerve through the hypoglossal canal; these are the axons of the hypoglossal nucleus en route to all tongue muscles except palatoglossus.

clinical.findings: Injury can cause ipsilateral tongue weakness and protrusion toward the weak side; denervation changes may develop over time. Contralateral motor/sensory signs indicate neighboring medial medullary pathway involvement.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, CN IX-XII, printed pp. 530-535 (PDF pp. 556-561).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), open medulla and cranial nerve nuclei, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).

name: Obex
synonyms: caudal apex of the fourth ventricle
function: Caudal apex of the fourth ventricle at its transition to the central canal, adjacent to the area postrema. It marks the transition between open and closed medulla, rather than the spinal cord-medulla junction.

clinical.findings: The obex is a dorsal medullary landmark relevant to lesions near the fourth-ventricle floor. Cerebellar tonsillar descent in Chiari assessment is measured relative to the basion-opisthion (McRae) line of the foramen magnum, not an obex-foramen-magnum line.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 12, brainstem surfaces, printed pp. 495-497 (PDF pp. 521-523).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), obex and medullary sections, printed pp. 112-118 (PDF pp. 126-132).
Congress of Neurological Surgeons, Guidelines for Chiari Malformation: Diagnosis (2023), https://www.cns.org/guidelines/browse-guidelines-detail/1-imaging.

name: Cerebellar hemispheres and vermis (context)
function: Cerebellar hemispheres joined by the midline vermis lie dorsal to pons and medulla. Lateral cortex participates in planning and coordination through dentate output; intermediate cortex connects to interposed nuclei; vermal and vestibular regions influence axial posture, gait, balance and eye movements. Lateral limb-control loops cross cerebellar output and later descending motor pathways, giving a predominantly ipsilateral relation to body coordination; medial outputs also have bilateral targets.

afferent: Crossed pontocerebellar fibers through the middle cerebellar peduncle (tract-mcp)
Olivocerebellar, spinocerebellar and vestibulocerebellar fibers through the inferior cerebellar peduncle (tract-icp)
Anterior spinocerebellar fibers through the superior cerebellar peduncle
efferent: Dentate/interposed output mainly through the superior cerebellar peduncle to contralateral thalamus and red nucleus
Fastigial/vestibulocerebellar output to vestibular and reticular nuclei through uncinate and juxtarestiform pathways

bloodSupply: Superior cerebellar artery (SCA) superiorly, anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) anteriorly, posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) inferiorly

clinical.findings: Hemispheric injury may cause ipsilateral appendicular dysmetria, intention tremor or impaired rapid alternating movements. Midline/vestibular injury may predominantly affect gait, trunk and eye movements. Lesion extent and connected pathways determine the actual combination.

contextNote: Context envelope for the 3D scene and sagittal/coronal plates (two hemispheres plus vermis bar); the deep nuclei and vermis are separate records, and the peduncles are owned elsewhere: tract-mcp (pons), tract-icp (medulla), tract-scp (midbrain).
refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar nuclei and connections, printed pp. 698-710 (PDF pp. 724-736).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medulla and inferior olive, printed pp. 112-121 (PDF pp. 126-135).

name: Dentate nucleus
function: The largest deep cerebellar nucleus, a convoluted gray ribbon in the lateral (neocerebellar) white matter: it collects inhibitory Purkinje output from the lateral hemispheres and fires the dentato-thalamo-cortical loop through the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral VL/VA thalamus and red nucleus — the efferent side of motor planning, movement timing and cognitive-linguistic sequencing.

afferent: Inhibitory Purkinje axons of the lateral cerebellar hemispheres
Excitatory collaterals of mossy-fiber and climbing-fiber afferents
efferent: Superior cerebellar peduncle (tract-scp) to contralateral VL thalamus and parvocellular red nucleus

bloodSupply: Superior cerebellar artery (SCA)

clinical.findings: Dentate injury can produce ipsilateral limb dysmetria and intention tremor. Output lesions above the SCP decussation instead affect the contralateral body; delayed tremor and other movement disorders vary by pathway extent.
Dentate or pre-crossing SCP injury can deafferent the contralateral inferior olive through dentato-rubro-olivary circuitry. Olivary MRI changes and palatal tremor are possible, not inevitable.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar nuclei and connections, printed pp. 698-710 (PDF pp. 724-736).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medulla and inferior olive, printed pp. 112-121 (PDF pp. 126-135).

name: Interposed nuclei (emboliform and globose)
function: Combined emboliform and globose nuclei of the intermediate (paravermal) spinocerebellum: they gate Purkinje output that compares intended with ongoing limb movement and fire the correction loop through the superior cerebellar peduncle to the magnocellular red nucleus (rubrospinal) and VL thalamus — the on-line limb stabilizer.

afferent: Inhibitory Purkinje output of intermediate/paravermal cortex
Excitatory mossy- and climbing-fiber collaterals
efferent: Crossed SCP output to contralateral VL thalamus and magnocellular red nucleus

bloodSupply: Deep cerebellar branches, often SCA-associated, with territorial variation.

clinical.findings: Interposed-nuclear injury can cause ipsilateral limb dysmetria and coordination difficulty. Tremor/tone/gait effects vary; preserved trunk or gait function cannot be assumed from an isolated label.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar nuclei and connections, printed pp. 698-710 (PDF pp. 724-736).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medulla and inferior olive, printed pp. 112-121 (PDF pp. 126-135).

name: Fastigial nucleus
function: Most medial deep cerebellar nucleus, receiving inhibitory Purkinje input mainly from the vermis. It influences balance, axial posture and eye-head coordination through bilateral vestibular and reticular targets, primarily along uncinate and juxtarestiform pathways; some output reaches the thalamus and tectum. The flocculonodular lobe also projects directly to vestibular nuclei.

afferent: Purkinje cells of cerebellar vermis
Mossy- and climbing-fiber collaterals
efferent: Bilateral vestibular and reticular nuclei through juxtarestiform and uncinate pathways
Thalamic and tectal targets through pathways associated with the superior cerebellar peduncle

bloodSupply: PICA (inferior) and SCA (superior) medial branches

clinical.findings: Fastigial or vermal lesions give a wide-based staggering gait with truncal instability and nystagmus while limb coordination on the bed may be preserved; bilateral posterior fossa lesions therefore present predominantly as gait ataxia.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar nuclei and connections, printed pp. 698-710 (PDF pp. 724-736).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medulla and inferior olive, printed pp. 112-121 (PDF pp. 126-135).

name: Vermis
function: The midline cerebellar strip separating the hemispheres on the dorsal surface, containing the vermal (axial body) representation of the spinocerebellum and, caudally, the uvula-nodulus of the vestibulocerebellum; governs trunk and proximal gait musculature and, with the nodulus-flocculus, gaze-holding and balance.

clinical.findings: Vermal injury can produce truncal/gait ataxia and imbalance, sometimes with ocular abnormalities. Limb coordination may be relatively preserved. Posterior-fossa tumors or degeneration are examples, but age, vomiting timing and examination patterns do not establish an etiology.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 15, cerebellar nuclei and connections, printed pp. 698-710 (PDF pp. 724-736).
Haines, Neuroanatomy: An Atlas of Structures, Sections, and Systems, 8th ed. (2012), medulla and inferior olive, printed pp. 112-121 (PDF pp. 126-135).

name: Medulla (context surface)
function: Context silhouette of medulla, including ventral pyramids, olives, dorsal gracile/cuneate tubercles and cranial root-exit sulci. The rostral open medulla contributes to the fourth-ventricle floor; the caudal closed medulla surrounds the central canal. Internal nuclei and pathways have separate records.
